title: LEBER OPTIC ATROPHY AND DYSTONIA
alt_titles: LEBER HEREDITARY OPTIC NEUROPATHY WITH DYSTONIA
DYSTONIA, FAMILIAL, WITH VISUAL FAILURE AND STRIATAL LUCENCIES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by homoplasmic or heteroplasmic mutation in the mitochondrially encoded MT-ND6 (516006), MT-ND4 (516003), MT-ND1 (516000), or MT-ND3 (516002) genes.

checks.claim: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by homoplasmic or heteroplasmic mutation in the mitochondrially encoded MT-ND6, MT-ND4, MT-ND1, or MT-ND3 genes.
checks.evidence_quote: The 3697G>A/ND1 mitochondrial DNA mutation causes the LHON and spastic dystonia phenotype in the same family.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports MT-ND1 as a cause and refers to earlier LHON-dystonia families with an ND6 mutation. It does not mention MT-ND4 or MT-ND3, and it does not say whether the mutations are homoplasmic or heteroplasmic. It only says the heteroplasmy level was measured.

paragraphs.text: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is a maternally inherited disorder in which vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia occur in variable combinations (Wang et al., 2009). Dystonia may be associated with subacute visual loss or asymptomatic optic atrophy and with bilateral symmetrical lucencies of the basal ganglia, especially the putamen (Marsden et al., 1986). The disorder is an oxidative phosphorylation disorder associated with complex I deficiency (Jun et al., 1996; De Vries et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2009).

checks.evidence_quote: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and dystonia (LDYT) is a mitochondrial disorder associated with variable combinations of vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia.
checks.explanation: Described as a mitochondrial disorder with affected individuals on the maternal side; 'maternally inherited' not explicitly stated.

checks.claim: In Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT), vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia occur in variable combinations.
checks.evidence_quote: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and dystonia (LDYT) is a mitochondrial disorder associated with variable combinations of vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia.

checks.claim: In Leber optic atrophy and dystonia, dystonia may be associated with subacute visual loss or asymptomatic optic atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: dystonia was variably associated with subacute visual loss or asymptomatic optic atrophy
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly. The paper calls the condition 'a unique disorder' and does not use the LDYT label.

checks.claim: In Leber optic atrophy and dystonia, dystonia may be associated with bilateral symmetrical lucencies of the basal ganglia, especially the putamen.
checks.evidence_quote: striking bilateral symmetrical lucencies on CT scan, especially involving the putamen
checks.explanation: The title calls these lucencies 'striatal', so placing them in the basal ganglia follows directly.

checks.claim: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia is an oxidative phosphorylation disorder associated with complex I deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: revealed a 60% reduction (P < 0.005) of complex I-specific activity in patient cell lines compared with controls
checks.explanation: Patient cells show a complex I deficiency. Complex I is an oxidative phosphorylation enzyme, so the 'oxidative phosphorylation disorder' label follows directly.

paragraphs.text: Gropman et al. (2004) reported a family with the G14459A mtDNA mutation and a broad range of clinical features. The proband was a 3-year-old girl with anarthria, dystonia, spasticity, and mild encephalopathy. Brain MRI showed bilateral, symmetric basal ganglia lucencies, and she had cerebral and systemic lactic acidosis. Her maternal first cousin had a much milder phenotype, with a new-onset limp and mild hemiparesis, and similar MRI findings.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-generation Hispanic family with LHON and/or dystonia, Jun et al. (1994) sequenced more than 90% of the mtDNA from a severely affected child and identified a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 14459 of the MT-ND6 gene, resulting in an ala72-to-val (A72V) substitution at a moderately conserved residue. The child's mtDNA belonged to Native American haplogroup D. The variant was not found in 38 Native American haplogroup D mtDNAs or in 108 Asian, 103 Caucasian, or 99 African mtDNAs. Six maternal relatives in 3 generations carried the mutation; 1 female with LHON was heteroplasmic. The authors suggested that it was the disease-causing mutation.

paragraphs.text: Jun et al. (1996) noted that the heteroplasmic G14459A mutation in MT-ND6 (A72V) had been identified as the cause of LHON and/or pediatric-onset dystonia in 3 unrelated families. Using transmitochondrial cybrids made by fusing enucleated patient lymphoblasts to an mtDNA-deficient (rho-0) lymphoblastoid line, they assigned the complex I defect to the 14459 mutation: mutant cybrids showed a 39% reduction (p less than 0.02) in complex I-specific activity relative to wildtype cybrids, with normal activity of other complexes. Kinetic analysis showed reduced Vmax with unchanged Km, and activity was inhibited by increasing concentrations of decylubiquinol, suggesting that the mutation may alter the coenzyme Q-binding site of complex I.

paragraphs.text: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) found none of the previously reported LHON mtDNA mutations. A muscle biopsy showed severe complex I deficiency.

checks.claim: The MT-ND3 10197G-A mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side of the Chinese LDYT family.
checks.evidence_quote: revealed a homoplasmy in the leukocytes of all the affected individuals on the maternal side.

checks.claim: Wang et al. (2009) noted that the MT-ND3 10197G-A mutation had also been reported in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The mtND3*10197A (m.10197G>A) mutation has recently been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.
